results.title: humane AI pin shuts down and discontinues all its call, text and smart conversation features
results.snippet:
Humane AI pin no longer works two years after its debut UPDATE (February 19th, 2025): Humane AI Pin announces it is shutting down and discontinuing all of its features, including calling, messaging, AI queries and responses, and cloud access. Less than two years after its debut, the hands-free device that has hoped to become a smartphone substitute no longer works. In a company note, the team says that every Humane AI Pin will officially stop working or operating starting February 28th, 2025, at 12pm PST. All users are encouraged to sync their stored pictures, videos, and notes before the date. ‘If you do not do this, your data will be lost upon deletion,’ the company writes. All the other consumer data will also be permanently deleted. On the date mentioned, the hands-free device stops connecting to Humane’s servers as its access fully retires. Effectively immediately as well is the discontinuation of selling the AI pin to new consumers.

device Humane unveils its AI Pin in a global debut on November 9th, 2023. Before the event, a series of snippets took place throughout the year to introduce the pin device, including co-founder Imran Chaudhri’s presentation and its appearance at the Coperni SS24 show in Paris. The wearable device is pinned to clothes using either magnets or a latch, and the cameras and sensors in front of it project app and other smartphone functionalities onto the user’s palm and surfaces. Humane AI Pin employs optical sensors that enable contextual and ambient compute interactions to make sensing-based technology work. The wearable projector and smartphone also function as a smart assistant using voice recognition. It can give accurate answers and carry out tasks for the user, doubling as a personal assistant. It integrates part of OpenAI’s ChatGPT and other software that enables the wearable AI assistant to reply to questions and do smartphone functions such as making calls, sending texts, and scheduling appointments using only the voice of the user. If privacy is an issue for the user, Humane AI Pin has a feature called ‘Trust Light’ where a light indicator switches on whenever the device’s sensors, microphone, and camera are recording.  Humane AI Pin finally makes its global debut as a wearable screenless smartphone Wearable smartphone for clothes that flash apps on hands Humane AI Pin is a stand-alone device. There is no need to connect the device to another smartphone or projector to make it work. It also heavily relies on gestures, which the user needs to learn to utilize the wearable device. For example, when it comes to listening to music, the user can ask the device to play a specific album. Then, they can project the program onto the palm of their hands. If they want to skip the song or listen to the previous track, they just need to tilt their hand to the left or right to activate this functionality. If they want to pause or play, they tilt their hand downward and make a ‘pinch’ gesture (the ‘pinch’ gesture is the equivalent of the swipe on smartphones). The user can not only ask Humane AI pin to send a message for them but also to use a certain tone in the way the message is written, be it excitement or nervousness. Before sending the message, the pin reads the text out loud and asks them if they are okay with it. Another feature is Catch Me Up where the wearable device reads through all the activities and reminders that the user has to finish and get done, acting like an assistant.

website Looking at the first batch’s design, the housing is made of (anodized) aluminum, and the available colors are white, silver, and black named Lunar, Equinox, and Eclipse respectively. The device’s head is stretched forward and slightly tilted, which helps the projection land straight onto the palm of the hands or at least be at the eye level of the user. Humane AI Pin’s steel-like casing might recall Apple’s iPhones with its singular block and reflective surface.

As of publishing the story, Humane AI pin will start accepting pre-orders starting November 16th at a price of 699 USD. The story is updated on February 19th, 2025 to report the device’s discontinuation.

results.title: Humane has killed its Ai Pin less than a year after its release
results.snippet:
[Humane's Ai Pin](https://mashable.com/article/ai-fail-meta-rabbit-humane) is about to become an expensive brick, with the startup set to discontinue service less than a year after the [wearable AI gadget began shipping](https://mashable.com/article/humane-ai-pin-reviews). It seems the fairy tale is over, and they can no longer deny that their golden carriage is actually a rotting pumpkin.
[In a post to Humane's support website](https://support.humane.com/hc/en-us/articles/34374173951373-Important-Update-for-Consumer-Ai-Pin-Customers), the company announced that all of its Ai Pins will stop working in just 10 days. All Ai Pins will stop connecting to Humane's servers on Feb. 28, and all customer data will be permanently deleted as well, with users instructed to download anything they don't want to lose before then. Humane has also ceased selling the gadget effective immediately.
"We are writing to inform you that, effective immediately, we are winding down the consumer Ai Pin as our business priorities have shifted," read Humane's post. "Your engagement has meant the world to us, and we deeply appreciate the role you’ve played in our innovation journey."
---
**You May Also Like**
---
---
Technically, the Ai Pin won't be completely useless. Humane notes that it will still offer offline features such as battery level. However, there's little point in checking how much battery is left on a gadget that only tells you how much battery it has left. Any of the Ai Pin's functions which require cloud connectivity will no longer work, including voice commands, AI responses — is basically anything you'd actually want to use the wearable for.
"We recognize that this may be an unexpected change, and we are here to support you," wrote Humane. This help is temporary though, as customer support for the Ai Pin will also be discontinued on Feb. 28.

You may be in luck if you bought a Humane Ai Pin within the last few months. [Humane states](https://support.humane.com/hc/en-us/articles/34243204841997-Ai-Pin-Consumers-FAQ) that Ai Pins which shipped on or prior to Nov. 15 are eligible for a refund, as they'll still be within the 90-day return window. However, you must submit your refund request by Feb. 27. If you purchased the Ai Pin but it hasn't shipped yet, you'll be refunded and your order automatically cancelled. Humane's mandatory subscriptions will also be automatically cancelled, with prepaid months refunded proportionately.
Unfortunately, anyone who has had their Ai Pin for longer has little recourse. Once the Ai Pins stop working, Humane advises customers to dispose of them via an [e-waste recycling program](https://mashable.com/feature/how-to-recycle-ewaste).

The Ai Pin's shutdown appears to be the result of [HP](https://mashable.com/category/hp) [acquiring "key AI capabilities" from Humane,](https://humane.com/media/humane-hp) which was also announced today. The $116 million acquisition includes Humane's [AI-powered operating system CosmOS](https://humane.com/cosmos), a swathe of intellectual property, and key technical personnel. Said employees will form HP's new AI innovation lab HP IQ.

Initially made available for [preorder in Nov. 2023](https://mashable.com/article/humane-launches-ai-pin-screenless-wearable-powered-openai), the Ai Pin aimed to supplant users' smartphones, and could perform functions such as taking photos, answering questions, and sending messages. Designed to pin to users' clothes, the then-$699 wearable was operated primarily via voice commands, and featured a tiny palm projector instead of a screen.
Unfortunately, issues began to arise before the Ai Pin was even released, with a promotional video showing [the Ai Pin answering questions incorrectly](https://mashable.com/article/humane-ai-pin-wrong-answers). Though Humane[ quickly updated the clip](https://mashable.com/article/humane-ai-pin-demo-video-updated-inaccuracy-blunders), numerous other problems with the Ai Pin [soon became apparent](https://mashable.com/article/humane-ai-pin-reviews) once users started getting their hands on the device in April last year. Users found the Ai Pin slow and frustrating to use, with issues ranging from broken music playback, to an unreadable projector display, to excessive heating up.
That isn't even to mention the problems with the [Ai Pin's charging case](https://mashable.com/article/humane-ai-pin-charging-case-fire-hazard), which was found to be a fire safety risk in June. Humane instructed its customers to stop using the charging case immediately, [subsequently recalling it](https://www.theverge.com/2024/10/31/24284691/humane-ai-pin-charge-case-recall-fire-hazard). Though the company initially offered replacements, in light of today's news it will now refund users "the portion of your original purchase price that was allocated to the Charge Case" instead.
Within less than five months from Humane's Ai Pins shipping,[ customers were reportedly returning the devices quicker than the company could sell them](https://mashable.com/article/humane-ai-pin-returns), and by October[ Humane had cut its price down to $499.](https://www.theverge.com/2024/10/23/24277964/humane-slashes-ai-pin-price-weak-sales)
[Humane reportedly began searching for a buyer](https://mashable.com/article/humane-ai-pin-selling) within mere weeks of shipping the Ai Pin, aiming to sell for $750 million to $1 billion. While its $116 million deal with HP isn't nothing, it's still a far cry from those lofty ambitions. And though Humane was able to offload its software, it looks like HP wants nothing to do with the Ai Pin hardware.

results.title: Humane Inc.
results.snippet:
Humane Inc. (stylized as hu.ma.ne) was an American consumer electronics company founded in 2018 by Imran Chaudhri and Bethany Bongiorno. The company designed and developed the AI Pin, a wearable voice-operated virtual assistant device, which started shipping in April 2024 but received poor reviews.

In February 2025, it was announced that HP would acquire most of Humane Inc. for $116 million. The deal includes the majority of Humane's employees, software platform, and intellectual property, including the AI Pin's CosmOS operating system and over 300 patents and patent applications, but excludes the AI Pin device business itself, which will be discontinued.

The AI Pin is a wearable device consisting of two separate parts—the front processing units and the rear battery. These parts are meant to be attached magnetically, sandwiching the user's clothing at chest level. It is a voice-activated AI assistant and cellular phone, equipped with a camera, speaker, motion sensors, and green monochrome 720p "Laser Ink" projector screen that motion detects the user's hand to project onto, indicated by a green light. The user mostly interacts with the device through a touchpad across most of its face and hand gestures in the air while the projection screen is active; the touchpad has to be tapped for it to listen for voice prompts. The AI and cloud storage features require a $24 monthly subscription. The device's only supported music streaming service is Tidal. Its operating system, CosmOS, is a custom Android distribution.

It was formally announced on November 9, 2023, and sales started one week later at a price of $699.

On October 23, 2024, Humane reduced the price of the AI Pin to $499 (excluding any charging case or spare battery).

In February 2025, Humane announced it had stopped selling the AI Pin and existing devices would no longer connect to the company’s servers after 12:00 AM San Francisco time on February 28. Following this, the device became virtually unusable and all consumer data on the company's servers was deleted.

The AI Pin has received generally negative reviews, praising its exterior design but criticizing its limited battery life and poor thermal control, and questioning the usefulness of many of its features. The New York Times reported that due to overheating problems, Humane executives would use ice packs to chill the AI Pin before previewing it to investors or partners. The author of the newspaper's Tech Fix column stated that the device had "glaring flaws" and was often "wrong, unhelpful or inefficient". The Verge wrote, "After many days of testing, the one and only thing I can truly rely on the AI Pin to do is tell me the time." Inverse stated that it "is slow to answer even basic questions." Fast Company noted that "Almost everything about the pin was a UX disaster for reviewers."

results.title: Humane AI Pin
results.snippet:
The **Humane AI Pin** was a screenless, wearable AI device developed by Humane Inc., a San Francisco startup founded by former Apple designers Imran Chaudhri and Bethany Bongiorno. Announced on November 9, 2023, and shipped to customers in April 2024, it was a small device that clipped magnetically to clothing and combined a voice assistant powered by [large language models](/wiki/large_language_model), a 13 MP camera, and a green "Laser Ink" projector that beamed a display onto the user's [palm](/wiki/palm). The AI Pin sold for $699 plus a mandatory $24 per month subscription through [T-Mobile](/wiki/t_mobile), and was marketed as a post-smartphone wearable that would let people use [artificial intelligence](/wiki/artificial_intelligence) without staring at a screen [1].
The AI Pin received some of the worst product reviews in recent technology history, then was discontinued less than a year after launch. Marques Brownlee (MKBHD), one of the most influential technology reviewers on [YouTube](/wiki/youtube), titled his review "The Worst Product I've Ever Reviewed... For Now" and concluded that the Pin was "bad at almost everything it does basically all the time" [2][3]. The device suffered from slow performance, frequent overheating, inaccurate AI responses, and short battery life. Humane sold roughly 10,000 units against an internal target of 100,000, and by mid-2024 returns had begun to outpace new sales [4][11].
On February 18, 2025, Humane announced it was shutting down and selling most of its assets, including its CosmOS software platform, more than 300 patents and patent applications, and much of its engineering team, to HP Inc. for about $116 million [5]. The AI Pin stopped functioning at 12:00 PM Pacific Time on February 28, 2025, when Humane permanently shut down its servers, bricking the devices and deleting customer data [5]. The combined story of a celebrated founding team, $230 million in funding, a historically bad launch, and a fire-sale acquisition has made the AI Pin one of the most cited cautionary tales in consumer AI hardware.
## Who founded Humane and how was it funded?
### Imran Chaudhri
Imran Chaudhri spent approximately 22 years at Apple, starting as an intern in 1995 in the Advanced Technology Group. During his tenure, he worked on the Mac, contributed to the creation of the iPhone, and was involved in the development of Apple Watch, HomePods, and AirPods. Chaudhri is credited with designing several key iPhone interface elements and was a named inventor on numerous Apple patents. He left Apple in 2017 to co-found Humane [1].

Humane first teased the AI Pin publicly during a TED talk by Imran Chaudhri in April 2023 at the Vancouver Convention Center. In a talk titled "The disappearing computer: and a world where you can take AI everywhere," Chaudhri demonstrated a prototype device clipped to his lapel that could project information onto his hand and respond to voice commands.

The full product was officially unveiled on November 9, 2023, at a dedicated launch event. The announcement revealed the $699 price point, the $24 per month T-Mobile subscription requirement, and the device's [feature set](/wiki/feature_set). Pre-orders opened one week later, with shipping scheduled for early 2024. The device began arriving to customers in April 2024.
## What were the Humane AI Pin's hardware and features?
The AI Pin was designed as a compact, screenless wearable intended to be worn on clothing at chest level.
### Physical design
The device consisted of two parts: the main unit containing the computing hardware, camera, and projector; and a detachable battery pack, called the Battery Booster, that attached magnetically through the user's clothing. This magnetic pass-through system meant the battery sat on the inside of the garment while the main unit faced outward. Humane sold additional Battery Boosters separately for $99 each, and users were expected to swap batteries throughout the day due to limited battery life. The device weighed approximately 55 grams (the main unit and one Battery Booster combined) and was available in three colors: Eclipse (black), Equinox (silver), and Lunar (gray) [1].
### Key specifications
| Component | Specification |
|---|---|
| Processor | Qualcomm Snapdragon (details not fully disclosed) |
| Camera | 13 MP ultra wide-angle (120 degree field of view) plus a 3D depth sensor |
| Projector | Green "Laser Ink" 720p monochrome display, Class 2 laser, usable at 20-40 cm |
| Connectivity | Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, 4G LTE (T-Mobile) |
| Storage | Cloud-based (Humane servers) |
| Interaction methods | Voice, touch gestures, laser projector, camera |
| Phone number | Dedicated T-Mobile number included with subscription |
| Weight | ~55 grams (main unit + Battery Booster) |
| Colors | Eclipse, Equinox, Lunar |
| Price | $699 device + $24 per month subscription |
| Battery Booster (extra) | $99 each |
### The Laser Ink Display
The AI Pin's most visually distinctive feature was its Laser Ink Display, a tiny green monochrome laser projector that could project text and simple graphics onto the user's palm or nearby flat surfaces. The display rendered a 720p image in bright greens and whites and was usable only at a distance of roughly 20 to 40 cm (about 8 to 16 inches) from the device.

The AI Pin ran Humane's proprietary Cosmos operating system (CosmOS) and used a combination of [AI models](/wiki/model) for its assistant capabilities. Touching the device and speaking activated the "AI Mic" feature, which could answer questions, translate languages, summarize information, and compose messages. The device integrated with [GPT-4](/wiki/gpt-4) for general knowledge queries and used [Microsoft](/wiki/microsoft) and Google services for search and other functions [7].
The camera could be used to identify objects, read text, provide nutritional information about food, and translate written text in real time. Humane marketed these as "Catch Me Up" (summarizing notifications), "AI Mic" (voice queries), and various gesture-based commands.

Humane had reportedly set an internal target of selling 100,000 AI Pin units. The actual sales figure was approximately 10,000 units, just 10% of the goal [4].

On February 18, 2025, Humane announced that it was shutting down and selling its assets to HP Inc. for $116 million. The deal represented a steep discount from the earlier $750 million to $1 billion asking price and fell well below the $230 million that investors had put into the company. For investors, the $116 million return on a $230 million+ investment represented a significant loss [5].

Humane announced that the AI Pin would permanently cease functioning at 12:00 PM Pacific Time on February 28, 2025. After that date, devices lost the ability to make calls, send messages, process AI queries, or access cloud storage. All user data stored on Humane's servers was permanently deleted, though customers were given the option to download their data beforehand. Customers whose devices had shipped on or after November 15, 2024 (within the previous 90 days) were eligible for a refund, but anyone who bought the device earlier was left with a non-functional piece of hardware that had cost them $699 [5].

As of early 2026, the Humane AI Pin no longer exists as a functioning product. All devices stopped working on February 28, 2025, when Humane's servers were permanently shut down. The technology and talent acquired by HP are being integrated into HP IQ, HP's AI innovation lab, with the goal of embedding AI capabilities into HP's existing product lines rather than building standalone AI hardware.

results.title: Humane Ai Pin · AI Entrepreneurship Wiki
results.snippet:
The Humane Ai Pin was a $699 screenless wearable AI device from Humane Inc. that, with a required $24/month subscription, routed spoken intent to cloud AI services - and lost its core functions on a single server-cutoff date when Humane shut the product down and sold its technology to HP.
The innovation
The Ai Pin pushed the screen and the app launcher off the device entirely, replacing them with an 'AI as router' layer (Cosmos/Ai Bus) that turned spoken intent into AI services - a genuinely new consumer form factor whose novelty also made it almost wholly dependent on the maker's cloud staying on.
## How the AI (or not) works
The Humane Ai Pin was built so that AI was the entire product. Humane unveiled it on November 9, 2023 as a wearable, conversational, and screenless device, available to order in the US from November 16 starting at $699 for the complete system [[1]](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/humane-launches-ai-pin---marking-a-new-beginning-for-personal-ai-devices-301983548.html). There was no display to tap through. Users spoke to it naturally, used a touchpad, made gestures, held up objects for its camera, or read a Laser Ink Display projected onto the palm, and the screenless interface was meant to blend into the background [[1]](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/humane-launches-ai-pin---marking-a-new-beginning-for-personal-ai-devices-301983548.html).
Underneath sat Cosmos, which Humane called its operating system for the AI era [[1]](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/humane-launches-ai-pin---marking-a-new-beginning-for-personal-ai-devices-301983548.html). Its Ai Bus framework was the distinguishing idea: it removed the need to download, manage, or launch apps, and instead tried to understand what the user needed and connect them to the right AI experience or service [[1]](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/humane-launches-ai-pin---marking-a-new-beginning-for-personal-ai-devices-301983548.html). That is the "AI as router" move: intent expressed in language, routed to a service, with no app launcher in between. The intelligence to do the routing did not live on the Pin. Humane's collaborations with Microsoft and OpenAI gave the device access to powerful external AI models, and the Pin was a standalone product running its own MVNO connected by exclusive US partner T-Mobile [[1]](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/humane-launches-ai-pin---marking-a-new-beginning-for-personal-ai-devices-301983548.html). The Pin reached general availability on April 11, 2024 [[2]](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/humane-announces-ai-pin-now-available-nationwide-302114323.html)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humane_AI_Pin).
By Humane's own description the Pin's AI features were delivered through cloud services and partner models: the launch release framed the OpenAI and Microsoft collaborations as giving the device access to powerful AI models, routed the AI work through the Ai Bus and the subscription's cloud services, and connected the device over its own T-Mobile-backed network [[1]](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/humane-launches-ai-pin---marking-a-new-beginning-for-personal-ai-devices-301983548.html).

Humane leaned hard on privacy framing. The Pin activated only on user engagement, used no wake words so it was not always listening, and carried a prominent Trust Light to signal when its sensors were active, managed by a dedicated privacy chip [[7]](https://www.theverge.com/news/614883/humane-ai-hp-acquisition-pin-shutdown).

The promise broke on a date. In February 2025, Humane told customers that the consumer Ai Pin would stop connecting to its servers after February 28, 2025 at 12pm PST, and that after that point the Pin's features would no longer include calling, messaging, AI queries and responses, or cloud access [[3]](https://support.humane.com/hc/en-us/articles/34374173951373-Important-Update-for-Consumer-Ai-Pin-Customers)[[4]](https://support.humane.com/hc/en-us/articles/34243204841997-Ai-Pin-Consumers-FAQ)[[7]](https://www.theverge.com/news/614883/humane-ai-hp-acquisition-pin-shutdown). The Verge, reporting on the same support documents, summarized it plainly: after the cutoff the Pins would "no longer connect to Humane's servers," and any function requiring cloud connectivity, such as voice interactions, AI responses, and .Center access, would stop, leaving only offline functions such as the battery-level readout [[4]](https://support.humane.com/hc/en-us/articles/34243204841997-Ai-Pin-Consumers-FAQ)[[7]](https://www.theverge.com/news/614883/humane-ai-hp-acquisition-pin-shutdown).

Humane said that at the same February 28 cutoff all remaining consumer data on its servers, including personally identifiable information, would be permanently deleted, and it urged users to download any stored photos, videos, and notes first [[3]](https://support.humane.com/hc/en-us/articles/34374173951373-Important-Update-for-Consumer-Ai-Pin-Customers)[[4]](https://support.humane.com/hc/en-us/articles/34243204841997-Ai-Pin-Consumers-FAQ). The recovery path for buyers was narrow. Refunds were offered only to customers still inside a 90-day return window (devices shipped on or after November 15, 2024), with all requests due by February 27, 2025, and subscriptions canceled with a prorated refund for any prepaid months past the cutoff [[4]](https://support.humane.com/hc/en-us/articles/34243204841997-Ai-Pin-Consumers-FAQ)[[7]](https://www.theverge.com/news/614883/humane-ai-hp-acquisition-pin-shutdown).

The shutdown was paired with a sale of the company's useful parts. On February 18, 2025, HP announced a definitive agreement to acquire key AI capabilities from Humane, namely the Cosmos platform, technical talent, and more than 300 patents and patent applications, in a $116 million transaction expected to close at the end of the month, with the team forming a new HP innovation lab called HP IQ [[5]](https://www.hp.com/us-en/newsroom/press-releases/2025/hp-accelerates-ai-software-investments-to-transform-the-future-of-work.html)[[7]](https://www.theverge.com/news/614883/humane-ai-hp-acquisition-pin-shutdown). The Verge described it directly as Humane "shutting down the AI Pin and selling its remnants to HP" [[7]](https://www.theverge.com/news/614883/humane-ai-hp-acquisition-pin-shutdown). The intelligence layer that made the Pin interesting moved into HP; the devices already on people's clothing did not come along.

The unresolved tension the Ai Pin leaves behind is about ownership. A buyer paid $699 for hardware and $24 a month for a service, but what they actually held was a thin client whose core jobs ran on someone else's servers [[1]](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/humane-launches-ai-pin---marking-a-new-beginning-for-personal-ai-devices-301983548.html)[[5]](https://www.hp.com/us-en/newsroom/press-releases/2025/hp-accelerates-ai-software-investments-to-transform-the-future-of-work.html). When the servers were switched off, the calling, messaging, AI answers, and cloud storage went with them, and the screenless design meant there was no familiar offline mode to retreat to [[4]](https://support.humane.com/hc/en-us/articles/34243204841997-Ai-Pin-Consumers-FAQ)[[7]](https://www.theverge.com/news/614883/humane-ai-hp-acquisition-pin-shutdown). The very feature that made the Pin distinctive — pushing the screen and the apps off the device and into an ambient AI router — is what left it with almost nothing to do once the router was gone [[3]](https://support.humane.com/hc/en-us/articles/34374173951373-Important-Update-for-Consumer-Ai-Pin-Customers)[[4]](https://support.humane.com/hc/en-us/articles/34243204841997-Ai-Pin-Consumers-FAQ)[[7]](https://www.theverge.com/news/614883/humane-ai-hp-acquisition-pin-shutdown).

results.title: Humane’s Ai Pin: What to Know
results.snippet:
Kocienda is the head of product engineering at Humane, a San Francisco company which, on Thursday, launched a device that its creators hope will be the iPhone for the AI generation. While the wearable computer, called the Humane Ai Pin, has a laser display that can be projected onto your hand if needed, the idea is that the device is screenless, instead conversing with its user in the form of speech. Its operating system calls upon AI large language models, including OpenAI’s GPT-4, for tasks as varied as calling a friend, translating a face-to-face conversation in real time, taking photographs, reminding you what your partner texted you last Thursday, or settling a dinnertime dispute about how many moons Jupiter has. The company is headed up by two former Apple executives, who helped design the iPhone and iPad, among other products. One of Humane’s biggest shareholders is OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who has previously said he believes an AI-first piece of consumer hardware is necessary to fully realize its benefits.

Part of Humane’s pitch is that the Pin will help liberate users from the tyranny of phone screens and the attention economy. “It’s a new kind of wearable device,” lead designer Imran Chaudhri said on stage at a TED talk in May, where he previewed the Pin for the first time. It allows you, he said, “to access the power of compute while remaining present in your surroundings, fixing a balance that’s felt out of place for some time now.”

I am welcomed in by Chaudhri and his wife Bethany Bongiorno, the co-founders of Humane, each of them wearing a Pin on their clothing. “What we’re seeing is that everyone’s really hungry for an AI-first platform—they just need the hardware that’s going to enable new experiences,” says Bongiorno, the company’s CEO. “It’s perfect timing.”

The Pin, which retails for $699 plus a $24 per month subscription fee, gives off the polished vibes of an Apple product—unsurprising, given many of Humane’s staff are former employees of the tech giant. (In 22 years at Apple, Chaudhri helped create the user interface for the iPhone among other devices. Bongiorno, a director of software engineering for iOS, was there for eight years.) Interacting with the Pin in truly natural language, rather than the stilted tones that last-generation virtual assistants like Siri or Alexa often require, seems to work well. As well as language, it can also cope with visual inputs, which a Humane staff member demonstrated to me by holding up an apple in front of him and asking the Pin if his diet plan would let him “eat this.” The Pin replied that it would.

On my visit, Kocienda asked his Pin to write him a haiku about the Golden Gate Bridge. It obliged with a passable poem, but one which didn’t fit the syllabic structure of a haiku. Because of how they’re built, systems like GPT-4 can make mistakes, or “hallucinate” information. And because they are probabilistic systems, not knowledge-retrieval systems, they can’t tell you how they know what they’ve told you is true—because they don’t. While the Pin has a clever operating system that can decide whether it’s better to do a web search for a question than ask a large language model, the voice-first interaction system often means that the source of the information is elided, meaning it’s hard, without following up, to assess how reliable a given answer is.

results.title: The Humane Ai Pin Has Already Been Brought Back to Life
results.snippet:
Humane bricked its pricey gadget on Friday afternoon. A short time later, a hacker got the codes to unlock it and potentially turn it into the true smartphone replacement it was meant to be.
Humane Ai Pin died, it was also reborn. Or at least, there was hope.
On February 28, shortly after noon Pacific time, Humane [switched off its servers](https://www.wired.com/story/what-to-do-with-your-humane-ai-pin/) supporting its contentious Ai Pin—essentially bricking a [$700 device](https://www.wired.com/review/humane-ai-pin/) that was less than a year old. Minutes later, in a Discord voice chatroom labeled “The death of Ai Pin,” one member of a band of dedicated hackers, determined to keep their Pins alive, let the rest of the group in on a secret. He had the codes they needed to get through Humane’s authentication.
Humane’s gadget has been the poster child of AI-enhanced hardware disappointments. The cute, clippable device was meant to hang on a lapel or shirt pocket and let you carry out many of the functions you’d find in a phone—take pictures, display text messages, and order around an AI chatbot, all with some added pizazz in the form of Humane’s promised holographic laser displays.
Released to the world in April 2024, the Pin was an immediate disappointment. Its main features simply [did not work well](https://www.wired.com/review/humane-ai-pin/), and from there things [just got worse](https://www.wired.com/story/things-keep-getting-worse-for-the-humane-ai-pin/). The Pin was a [resounding flop](https://www.wired.com/story/revisiting-the-three-biggest-flops-of-2024/), widely mocked, and the company even reached the point where it [processed more returns](https://www.theverge.com/2024/8/7/24211339/humane-ai-pin-more-daily-returns-than-sales) of the device than it had sold. In February 2025, less than a year after the Pin was released, Humane announced it would [shut down its services](https://humane.com/media/humane-hp) at the end of the month—Friday, February 28—and part off some of its key AI components to the computer company HP. Humane offered few concessions to Pin owners. Refunds [would only be given](https://support.humane.com/hc/en-us/articles/34243204841997-Ai-Pin-Consumers-FAQ) if someone had purchased a Pin within the past 90 days.
For the remaining fans of the expensive, short-lived device, the move was a gut punch. In the final week of the Humane Ai Pin’s short life, soon-to-be-former users ran through all of the stages of grief across Humane’s subreddits and Discord servers. There were furious rebukes. Heartbroken goodbyes. Disappointment all around.

The Humane Ai Pin runs an instance of Android as its OS, which means in theory the system could be debugged and have custom apps sideloaded onto it. But the Pin needed to be able to connect to another computer to do that. Since Humane’s service was being shut down, wireless features wouldn’t work—so it had to be a wired connection. But the Humane Ai Pin has no obvious ports, so finding a way to plug it in wasn't immediately apparent.
In a Discord channel dedicated to modifying the Pin, users quickly figured out how to uncover the hidden DIM connectors—they were covered with a moon-shaped sticker of Humane’s logo—that would enable a wired connection from the Pin to a computer. The problem was, the connectors were tiny, barely 1 millimeter apart, and nobody had any other cords that would fit. After trying several different connector types, Marcel and other tinkerers opted to create their own. Marcel sliced up four different USB cables looking for one with the right wires that could connect to the sensors on the Pin. He soldered them on, plugged the other end of the cord into his computer, and had them connected. Maybe this wasn't the end after all.
But there was another problem. Humane shutting down services meant it would brick the device completely, making the operating system on the Pin inaccessible. Without an authentication certificate to open the OS, owners who had managed to get it hooked up to their computers were greeted with an impassable screen. Marcel, and the community at large, were stuck. It was technically possible to hack it—the right geek can hack just about anything eventually—but getting through that authentication was a different matter.

Brendan Brannock, a 30-year-old network engineer in Florida also working on a way to connect with his Humane Pin, put together a knowledge base document to help other people in the community start tinkering with their devices. He found a compatible wiring device on Amazon that would connect to the Humane Pin’s port and fiddled his way into building a 3D model of a base that would hold the connection in place.

Humane owners on the reHumane Discord had wanted the company to put out an OTA—an over-the-air update that would enable them to access the OS on the device. Humane, in its downward spiral toward dissolution, didn’t outwardly make any moves to do that.
Still, the word got out, and shortly after the device was shut down on February 28, Marcel had an announcement. Somebody from Humane—he would never say who—had slipped him and a few other users an internal certificate used by employees that would grant access to the Pin.
In the Discord voice chat, Marcel broke the news by sharing his screen and playing a video. In it, he held out his hand, and across his palm the Humane Ai Pin’s laser projector played the music video for Nomico’s “Bad Apple,” which has become a meme as the first video hackers put on a jailbroken device. The chat went wild. The Ai Pin was theirs.

However, a Humane employee, who requested anonymity due to not being authorized to speak publicly on such matters, also expressed his frustrations with the community's actions. He pointed out that using proprietary access certifications without permission is an IP violation—one that HP, which now owns Humane’s IP, may or may not want to pursue.

results.title: AI Pin review and score · wearable.tools
results.snippet:
Humane's AI Pin had the best privacy hardware anyone has shipped in this category and was remotely bricked on 28 February 2025, which is the only fact that now matters.

| Capture | 23% | 5.0 | 1.15 | Humane's AI Pin used a dual microphone array and activated only on deliberate touch, which made it reliable for commands and useless for capturing a conversation you did not initiate. |
| Intelligence | 17% | 3.5 | 0.60 | Humane's AI Pin activated on a touch and needed no phone thanks to LTE, but every query routed through CosmOS, so when the servers went dark on 28 February 2025 the device retained essentially no capability. |
| Privacy | 16% | 8.5 | 1.36 | Humane's AI Pin drove its Trust Light from a dedicated privacy chip that would shut the device down if tampered with, and used no wake word — the strongest such design yet shipped. |
| Battery | 14% | 2.0 | 0.28 | Reviewers measured about four hours on Humane's AI Pin itself and nine with the Battery Booster, so a full day meant physically hot-swapping batteries. |
| Wearability | 12% | 3.0 | 0.36 | Humane's AI Pin weighed 34.2 g and clipped on via a 20.5 g Battery Booster, so roughly 54.7 g hung on a shirt, and reviewers reported thermal shutdowns against the skin. |
| Look | 7% | 4.5 | 0.32 | Humane's AI Pin was designed as a square clip-on block rather than as jewellery, so on a shirt it read as a piece of consumer electronics, not as a pin you would otherwise wear. |
| Value | 11% | 0.0 | 0.00 | Humane's AI Pin cost $499 plus a mandatory $24 a month, around $787 in year one, for a device that no longer functions at all. |

What works
- The Trust Light was governed by a dedicated privacy chip that shut the device down if compromised
- No wake word at all — it activated only on deliberate touch
- An eSIM over LTE made it the only device here that worked with no phone at all
- A projector, a 13 MP camera and a localised speaker, none of which anything here has matched
What does not
- Bricked on 28 February 2025 at 12pm PST, with all remaining user data permanently deleted
- The $24/month subscription was mandatory; lapse it and the hardware became inoperable
- Around four hours of battery, requiring you to hot-swap boosters to get through a day
- The Charge Case was recalled over a battery fire risk

A 34.2 g pin with two microphones, a 13 MP camera, depth and motion sensors, a 720p laser projector that painted an interface onto your palm, and a “personic” speaker that used HRTF to put a bubble of sound where only the wearer could hear it. An eSIM on Humane’s own MVNO meant it needed no phone. There was deliberately no mobile app at all; everything ran through a website.
The privacy hardware was better than anything shipped before or since. The Trust Light — a bar of three RGB LEDs — was driven by a dedicated privacy chip, and if that chip detected compromise the Pin would shut down and require service. There was no wake word; Humane’s own launch materials stated the device “only activates upon user engagement”, so it was not listening between interactions.

HP acquired Humane’s CosmOS platform, 300-plus patents and the engineering team for $116 million, announced on 18 February 2025. Sales stopped that day. Ten days later, at 12pm PST on 28 February, the Pins stopped connecting to Humane’s servers — taking with them calling, messaging, AI queries and cloud access, which is to say all of it — and remaining consumer data was permanently deleted. Refunds were limited to purchases inside a 90-day shipping window, with claims due the day before the shutdown.
There is a postscript worth recording, because it is the part that does not usually get written down. Checked on 16 September 2026, neither `humane.com` nor `support.humane.com` resolves in DNS at all. The shutdown notice Humane posted for its own customers is gone, along with the specification page. Every figure on this page is therefore cited to Humane’s launch release on a wire service or to contemporaneous reporting, because the manufacturer’s account of its own product no longer exists on the internet. When a device in this category dies, the documentation dies with it.
The subscription was structural to this, not incidental. At $24 a month it was mandatory, and lapsing it made the hardware inoperable before Humane ever shut anything down. A $499 device with a hard dependency on a monthly payment to a single startup was never yours in the sense buyers assumed.

results.title: Humane AI Pin: Why It Failed
results.snippet:
StatusSales ended February 18, 2025; Humane said the Pins would go offline February 28, 2025
Humane's AI Pin was a screenless wearable built around an AI assistant, priced from $699. It reached buyers in April 2024, and Humane stopped selling it 10 months later, on the day HP agreed to buy Humane's key AI capabilities for $116 million.
## What it was
The Humane AI Pin was a wearable you controlled by voice, touchpad and gesture, with a laser display projected onto your palm in place of a screen.
Instead of apps and a keyboard, [The Verge's review](https://www.theverge.com/24126502/humane-ai-pin-review) said, it put everything behind an AI assistant and an operating system Humane called CosmOS.
The Pin didn't need a phone. It ran on Humane's own mobile service through T-Mobile, and Humane's subscription page said you had to pay for that service, $24 a month, to use it.
Humane announced the Pin on November 9, 2023, starting at $699 for the complete system. TechCrunch later wrote that Humane positioned it as a smartphone replacement.
Humane was a Bay Area startup founded by Imran Chaudhri and Bethany Bongiorno, both formerly of Apple. Bongiorno was its CEO.
## What happened
The AI Pin shipped late to scathing reviews, and within weeks, The New York Times reported, Humane was in talks to sell itself.
Its ship date slipped from March to mid-April 2024, TechCrunch reported. The Verge's review, published April 11, said "it just doesn't work". Marques Brownlee called it "the worst product I've ever reviewed", The Verge reported.
By early April, Humane had around 10,000 orders against the 100,000 it hoped to sell that year, [The New York Times reported](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/06/06/technology/humane-ai-pin.html). About a week after the reviews, according to the same report, Humane started talking to HP about selling itself for more than $1 billion.
Between May and August 2024, more AI Pins were returned than bought, according to [internal sales data The Verge obtained](https://www.theverge.com/2024/8/7/24211339/humane-ai-pin-more-daily-returns-than-sales). A source put the number still in customers' hands closer to 7,000.

In October 2024, Humane cut the price by $200, to $499, TechCrunch reported. It also recalled about 10,500 of the Pin's charging cases over overheating concerns, The Verge reported.
On February 18, 2025, [HP announced](https://www.hp.com/us-en/newsroom/press-releases/2025/hp-accelerates-ai-software-investments-to-transform-the-future-of-work.html) a $116 million deal for Humane's AI platform, technical staff and more than 300 patents and patent applications. The same day, Humane [told customers](http://web.archive.org/web/20250219110309/https://support.humane.com/hc/en-us/articles/34374173951373-Important-Update-for-Consumer-Ai-Pin-Customers) it was winding the Pin down and ending sales effective immediately.
Humane said the Pins would lose calls, messages, AI answers and cloud access at 12pm PST on February 28, 2025. The Verge reported in May 2025 that Humane had "shut down all AI Pins in February".

The Verge's David Pierce reported that the Pin couldn't set an alarm or a timer, and that routing every request through Humane's servers made it "at best quite slow and at worst a total failure". Using it for more than a couple of minutes, he got an overheating warning. A Pin and a battery booster went from fully charged to dead in five hours, untouched in his backpack.
